Solution

i OurBigBook.com
For congruence classes in Z/NZ, define
[a]+[b]=[a+b],[a][b]=[ab].​
(1)
These operations are independent of representatives. If a′=a+Nr and b′=b+Ns, then (a′+b′)−(a+b)=N(r+s) and a′b′−ab=N(rb+sa+Nrs). Thus changing representatives leaves both results in the same congruence class. The usual integer laws descend to make this a commutative ring with zero [0] and identity [1].

The decimal expansion gives M=∑i=0s​ai​10i. In modular arithmetic, 10≡−1(mod11), and hence
M≡i=0∑s​(−1)iai​(mod11).​
(2)
An integer is divisible by eleven exactly when its congruence class is zero, proving both directions of the alternating-digit test.

i OurBigBook.com
The Baire category theorem says that a countable intersection of open dense sets in a nonempty complete metric space is dense. Write E={e1​,e2​,…}. Each singleton is closed in a metric space and has empty interior because there are no isolated points. Therefore every X∖{ej​} is open and dense. Applying the theorem also to G yields
G∖E=G∩⋂j≥1​(X∖{ej​}),
(3)
which is dense in X. Thus every nonempty open subset meets the required difference, not merely the original dense set G.

No. Take the complete metric space X=R with its usual metric, E=Q, and G=Q∪(1,2). This G is uncountable and dense, whereas
G∖E=(1,2)∖Q
(4)
misses, for example, the nonempty open interval (3,4). Uncountability does not replace the open-dense hypothesis in the Baire category theorem.

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 152
3F OurBigBook.com
A plane plane crystallographic group is a discrete subgroup of the Euclidean isometry group with compact quotient. Its translations form a normal rank-two Euclidean lattice Λ; this is the standard translation-lattice structure of a plane crystallographic group. Its point group is the finite group of linear parts, equivalently the quotient by those translations. Conjugating a translation by an isometry sends its translation vector to its image under the linear part, so every point-group element preserves Λ.
Choose a Euclidean lattice basis. A rotational linear part is then represented by an integer matrix A, since it sends the basis to Euclidean lattice vectors. In an orthonormal basis the same map has eigenvalues eiθ,e−iθ, and its trace is independent of basis. Thus
2cosθ=trA∈Z∩[−2,2]={−2,−1,0,1,2}.
(5)
These possibilities give rotation angles, modulo a full turn, π, ±2π/3, ±π/2, ±π/3, and 0, respectively. Consequently the crystallographic restriction theorem is
rotation order ∈{1,2,3,4,6}.​
(6)
The restriction comes from integrality of the Euclidean lattice action, not simply from finiteness of the point group.

Solution

4H OurBigBook.com
A binary uniquely decodable code assigns a finite binary word to each source symbol, so that no two distinct finite sequences of source symbols have the same concatenated encoding. This does not require the stronger prefix property. All codeword lengths are positive.
Put S=∑j​2−lj​ and let Ak,L​ count sequences of k source symbols whose encoded total length is L. Expanding the product gives
Sk=∑L=klmin​klmax​​Ak,L​2−L.
(7)
Unique decodability makes these encodings distinct, so Ak,L​≤2L, the number of binary strings of that length. There are at most k(lmax​−lmin​)+1 possible lengths. Therefore
Sk≤k(lmax​−lmin​)+1.
(8)
Taking kth roots and letting k→∞ proves the McMillan inequality:
j∑​2−lj​≤1.​
(9)

5J OurBigBook.com
Independence in the Bernoulli logistic-regression model gives the log-likelihood
ℓ(β)=∑i=1n​[yi​βxi​−log(1+eβxi​)].
(10)
Writing μi​=(1+e−βxi​)−1, the score function and curvature are
ℓ′(β)=i∑​xi​(yi​−μi​),ℓ′′(β)=−i∑​xi2​μi​(1−μi​).​
(11)
Thus a finite maximum-likelihood estimate solves ∑i​xi​(yi​−μ​i​)=0. If at least one xi​=0, the curvature is strictly negative for finite β, so any such solution is the unique maximizer.
Use the Newton method, which here coincides with Fisher scoring because the second derivative does not depend on the observed responses:
βk+1​=βk​+∑i​xi2​μi​(βk​)(1−μi​(βk​))∑i​xi​(yi​−μi​(βk​))​.
(12)
Step damping or a bracket for the monotone score provides reliable numerical convergence. If all covariates are zero the parameter is unidentifiable; if the outcomes are separated in the direction of the covariates, the likelihood supremum may occur at β=+∞ or −∞ rather than at a finite estimate.

6A OurBigBook.com
The positive steady state satisfies 1+b(N∗)2=r, so
N∗=(r−1)/b​.​
(13)
With Nt​=N∗+ηt​, the linearization is
ηt+1​=ηt​−r2(r−1)​ηt−1​.
(14)
Its characteristic polynomial is λ2−λ+d, where d=2(r−1)/r. The roots are inside the unit disk precisely when 0<d<1: when they are real they are positive with sum one, and when complex conjugate their common modulus is d​. Therefore the fixed point is linearly asymptotically stable for 1<r<2 and unstable for r>2. At r=2,
λ±​=e±iπ/3,ηt+6​=ηt​.​
(15)
This proves period six for the neutral linearized oscillations. The stronger printed claim of a nonlinear period-six branch is not valid for the stated recurrence. It is important to distinguish these two assertions.
Here is a local obstruction, which also checks that the qualification is not merely absence of a proof. Normalize by the moving fixed point, let x=Nt−1​/N∗(r)−1, y=Nt​/N∗(r)−1, and define
Fr​(x,y)=(y,1+(r−1)(1+x)2r(1+y)​−1).
(16)
Put v=(x,y)T, δ=r−2, and Q=x2−xy+y2>0 for v=0. The quadratic and cubic terms of F2​'s second component are x2/2−xy+x2y/2. Composing six times gives
Fr6​(v)−v=δBv+QDv+O(∣v∣4+∣δ∣∣v∣2+δ2∣v∣),B=(1−1​12​),D=(−1/21​−1−3/2​).
(17)
In particular the quadratic terms cancel, while the cubic components are −(x+2y)Q/2 and (2x−3y)Q/2. If a small nonzero v were a period-six point, invertibility of B and the norm of this equation would imply ∣δ∣=O(∣v∣2). Taking its determinant with Bv then gives
0=det(Bv,QDv)+O(∣v∣5)=2Q2​+O(∣v∣5).
(18)
Since Q≥∣v∣2/2, this is impossible for sufficiently small nonzero v. Thus no nontrivial nonlinear six-cycle bifurcates locally at r=2. At the threshold the same expansion gives Q(F26​(v))=Q(v)−2Q(v)2+O(∣v∣5), so the fixed point is actually locally asymptotically stable nonlinearly, with slow decay. The valid intended linear-stability conclusion is the period-six neutral oscillation above; a literal nonlinear assertion requires a changed model or wording. This is an example of the distinction between linear resonance and nonlinear periodic bifurcation.

Solution

Words: 229
7D OurBigBook.com
The nullclines are y=μx and y=x2/[ν(1+x2)]. At a nonzero fixed point, cancellation of x yields μν=x/(1+x2). The latter function attains its maximum 1/2 at x=1. Hence
μc​=2ν1​,O=(0,0),P±​=(x±​,μx±​),x±​=2μν1±1−4μ2ν2​​.​
(19)
For 0<μ<μc​, x−​<1<x+​ and x−​x+​=1.
The Jacobian matrix is
J(x,y)=(−μ2x/(1+x2)2​1−ν​).
(20)
At O the distinct eigenvalues are −μ,−ν, so the origin is a stable node. At a nonzero fixed point its trace is −(μ+ν)<0 and
detJ=μν1+x2x2−1​.
(21)
The discriminant is (μ−ν)2+8x/(1+x2)2>0. Thus P−​ is a saddle and P+​ is a stable node, never a focus.
Above the straight nullcline x˙>0; below it x˙<0. Below the curved nullcline y˙​>0; above it y˙​<0. At the saddle, an eigenvector can be chosen as (1,μ+λ): the stable eigenvalue gives negative slope, and the unstable eigenvalue gives positive slope. The stable manifold is the basin boundary. The two branches of the unstable manifold lead respectively to the origin and the positive stable node, as illustrated for representative parameters.
The nonnegative quadrant is forward invariant. Since y˙​≤1−νy, y stays bounded, and then x˙=−μx+y also bounds x. Moreover the divergence is the negative constant −(μ+ν), excluding periodic or homoclinic loops by the Bendixson-Dulac criterion. The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem then leaves convergence to a fixed point. Initial data on the saddle's stable manifold approach the saddle; data in the two open basins approach extinction at O or persistence at P+​, respectively.

The real part of a holomorphic function is real analytic and has a local complexification in its two real coordinates. Define f∗(w)=f(wˉ)​. On real (x,y),
2u(x,y)=f(x+iy)+f∗(x−iy),
(22)
and the same identity holds after analytic continuation to complex (x,y). Substituting x=(z+zˉ0​)/2 and y=(z−zˉ0​)/(2i) gives x+iy=z and x−iy=zˉ0​, hence
f(z)=2u(2z+zˉ0​​,2iz−zˉ0​​)−f(z0​)​.​
(23)
The conjugation on the final constant is present in the PDF but was lost in the converted TeX. Without it the formula already fails when z=z0​ and f(z0​) is not real.
Now zeiz=(x+iy)e−y(cosx+isinx) has the specified real part. Thus the complete family is
f(z)=zeiz+iC,C∈R.​
(24)
Any two such holomorphic functions differ by a holomorphic function with zero real part; the Cauchy-Riemann equations make its imaginary part constant on a connected neighborhood.

Solution

Words: 110
9D OurBigBook.com
In Lagrangian mechanics, the energy balance for an autonomous Lagrangian uses E=∑i​q˙​i​∂L/∂q˙​i​−L. For the stationary vector potential the velocity-linear magnetic term cancels in this expression, leaving kinetic energy. In cylindrical coordinates,
L=2m​(r˙2+r2ϕ˙​2+z˙2)+er2g(z)ϕ˙​.
(25)
Time independence and the cyclic angular coordinate give two constants:
E=2m​(r˙2+r2ϕ˙​2+z˙2),pϕ​=mr2ϕ˙​+er2g(z).​
(26)
The three Euler-Lagrange equations are
mr¨=mrϕ˙​2+2ergϕ˙​,dtd​(mr2ϕ˙​+er2g)=0,mz¨=er2g′ϕ˙​.
(27)
The supplied angular velocity is ϕ˙​=−2eg(z0​)/m. Set r=r0​, z=z0​ and use this constant angular velocity. The radial right-hand side is mr0​(ϕ˙​2+2egϕ˙​/m)=0, the angular momentum is constant, and the vertical equation vanishes when g′(z0​)=0. These equations and the initial data therefore give
r(t)=r0​,z(t)=z0​,ϕ(t)=ϕ0​−m2eg(z0​)​t.​
(28)
For nonzero radius and charge this is the requested circular orbit.

10D (Cosmology)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
10D OurBigBook.com
The Hubble time is the instantaneous inverse expansion rate H0−1​, where H=a˙/a. A radial light ray covers comoving distance ∫cdt/a(t). Since a(t0​)=1, the present proper radius of the particle horizon is
R0​=c∫0t0​​a(t)dt​.​
(29)
For the power-law scale factor, a(0)=0 requires α>0. The integral converges only when α<1, in which case
R0​=1−αct0​​,H0​=t0​α​,t0​=αH0−1​.​
(30)
At α=1 the divergence is logarithmic, and at α>1 it is a power divergence. The familiar flat-universe epochs have α=1/2 for radiation and α=2/3 for pressureless matter, obtained from ρ∝a−4 or a−3 and the Friedmann equation. Both have 0<α<1, so their ages are less than the present Hubble time. These power laws describe idealized single-component epochs rather than the full late-time expansion history.

11F OurBigBook.com
Inversion in a circle of center c and radius R is K(z)=c+R2/(zˉ−cˉ) on the extended plane. It sends infinity to c, so it interchanges zero and infinity exactly when c=0.
For the unit-circle inversion J, both J and K are involutions. If KJz0​=z0​, applying K gives Jz0​=Kz0​. Writing w=Jz0​, we have Jw=z0​ and Kw=z0​, and therefore KJw=Kz0​=w. This proves both assertions about the fixed points.
We now show that one fixed point is inside the disk and use it as the hyperbolic center. Rotate coordinates to make the Euclidean center c=a≥0. The hypothesis is a+R<1. If a=0 the conclusion follows immediately from the radial hyperbolic distance. If a>0, then
T(z)=a+1−azR2z​,az2−(1+a2−R2)z+a=0
(31)
for its fixed points. Since 1+a2−R2>2a, this quadratic has two positive roots with product one, one p∈(0,1) and the other 1/p>1.
The disk automorphism h(z)=(z−p)/(1−pz) is a Poincare disc automorphism. It sends the two fixed points to zero and infinity and commutes with J on the extended plane. Consequently K′=hKh−1=(hTh−1)J interchanges zero and infinity. Conjugation takes circle inversion to inversion in the image circle, so the first part says that h(Γ) is centered at zero. Its Euclidean radius is some s<1.
In the Poincaré disk metric, integrating the radial length element gives
dD​(0,z)=∫0∣z∣​1−r22dr​=2artanh∣z∣.
(32)
Since h preserves distance, the original circle is exactly
Γ={z∈D:dD​(p,z)=2artanhs}.​
(33)
Undoing the preliminary rotation gives the center for arbitrary complex c.
This identifies the hyperbolic circle in the Poincare disc intrinsically.

12H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 425 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 425
12H OurBigBook.com
A binary symmetric channel flips each transmitted bit independently with probability p. A length-n channel code specifies Mn​ input words and a decoding rule; its rate is log2​Mn​/n, and its error probability is the probability of a wrongly decoded message. The channel capacity is the supremum of asymptotically achievable rates with vanishing error. For 0≤p≤1, put h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p), with 0log2​0=0. The Shannon second coding theorem here states
C=1−h2​(p)bits per channel use.​
(34)
We prove achievability and the converse rather than using the formula as a substitute for a coding argument. Output complementation reduces p>1/2 to 1−p, so first assume 0<p<1/2.
Fix R<C. Choose δ>0 such that q=p+δ<1/2 and R<1−h2​(q). Independently choose Mn​=⌊2nR⌋ uniformly random input words. Decode a received word to the unique codeword within Hamming distance ⌊nq⌋, declaring error if there is none or more than one. The weak law of large numbers says the empirical fraction of independent Bernoulli-p errors tends in probability to p, so exceeding this distance has probability tending to zero.
For any independently chosen competing codeword, its probability of lying in this ball is 2−nBn​(q), where
Bn​(q)=∑j≤nq​(jn​)≤(n+1)2nh2​(q).
(35)
Indeed (jn​)≤2nh2​(j/n) follows by bounding the probability of exactly j successes in a binomial experiment with parameter j/n by one, and h2​ increases on [0,1/2]. A union bound therefore bounds the ensemble-average decoding error by
P{Bin(n,p)>nq}+(n+1)2−n(1−h2​(q)−R)⟶0.
(36)
Some deterministic code is at least as good as this average. Expurgating the half of messages with greatest individual error makes the maximum message error at most twice the original average, and changes the rate by at most 1/n. This proves achievability even for maximum-error probability.
For the converse, take uniform messages and any deterministic code/decoder. The independent noise word Z has probability p∣Z∣(1−p)n−∣Z∣. Its normalized negative log-probability tends in probability to h2​(p) by the same law. Thus, outside an event of probability tending to zero, each noise word has probability at most 2−n(h2​(p)−δ). The decoder's disjoint decision regions Dj​ contain at most 2n received words in total. Hence
Psuccess​≤o(1)+Mn​1​∑j​∣Dj​∣2−n(h2​(p)−δ)≤o(1)+2n(1−Rn​−h2​(p)+δ).
(37)
At rates bounded above capacity by a positive amount, choose smaller δ and obtain success probability tending to zero. This establishes the strong converse as well as the ordinary impossibility of reliable transmission above C.
When p=1/2 the output is independent of the input, so success probability for uniform messages is at most 1/Mn​ and C=0. At p=0 or 1 the channel is noiseless or deterministically inverted; all 2n words can be distinguished, so C=1. These endpoints complete the theorem.

Let ℓsat​ denote the maximized log-likelihood in the saturated model, with one fitted mean per observation. With known dispersion, define the deviance of a fitted model as D=2(ℓsat​−ℓfitted​); for an exponential-dispersion convention that scales deviance by the dispersion ϕ, divide that scaled quantity by ϕ in the following test.
Let D0​,D1​ be the fitted deviances under the null and full models. Their difference is the likelihood-ratio test statistic
D0​−D1​=2(ℓ(β​)−ℓ(β​0​,0)).​
(38)
Under the regular identifiable interior null hypothesis, Wilks theorem gives the limiting χp−p0​2​ distribution. Reject for an observed difference above its chosen upper-tail critical value. This concerns the difference of fitted model deviances, not simply the full-model deviance compared with zero.
For a Poisson regression, the means are μi​=exiT​β and ℓ=∑i​(yi​logμi​−μi​−logyi​!). Saturation sets μi​=yi​, taking the limiting value at yi​=0. Consequently the Poisson deviance is
D=2i∑​[yi​logμ​i​yi​​−(yi​−μ​i​)],​
(39)
with 0log0=0. The intercept score implies ∑i​(yi​−μ​i​)=0 at a finite fit, although retaining that term makes the individual deviance contributions clear.
For yi​=μ​i​+δi​ with ∣δi​∣/μ​i​ small, expand (μ​i​+δi​)log(1+δi​/μ​i​)−δi​. The linear term cancels and the result is δi2​/(2μ​i​)+O(∣δi​∣3/μ​i2​). Therefore
D≃∑i​μ​i​(yi​−μ​i​)2​,
(40)
the Pearson chi-squared statistic. The approximation requires adequately large fitted counts and small relative residuals; it is not an identity for sparse observations.

Rapid decay allows two integrations by parts in the half-line Fourier transform. They give
∂t​u+ωu=−ux​(0,t)−(ik+β)u(0,t).

Solving this scalar inhomogeneous equation by an integrating factor yields
u(k,t)=e−ωtu(k,0)−(ik+β)f0​(ω,t)−f1​(ω,t).​

The boundary transforms are entire in k; with the standard smooth, compatible boundary data, integration by parts in the time integral gives the required polynomial bounds. Let the stellar radius be R and assume zero external surface pressure. A spherical shell has mass dm=4πr2ρdr and contributes −Gm(r)dm/r to the gravitational potential energy. Using hydrostatic pressure support,
Egrav​=−∫0R​4πGmρrdr=4π∫0R​r3P′dr=−12π∫0R​r2Pdr=−3⟨P⟩V​.

The total energy is (α−3)⟨P⟩V, so energetic gravitational binding requires α<3. For an isotropic gas, kinetic theory gives P=(1/3)∫pvdn. Nonrelativistic kinetic energy is pv/2, giving U=3PV/2 and α=3/2. Ultrarelativistic energy is pv, giving U=3PV and α=3: the ultrarelativistic limit is marginal in this Newtonian virial balance.
For a white dwarf, electron degeneracy pressure becomes ultrarelativistic as density increases. Its equation of state then scales as P=Kρ4/3. Pressure support and gravitational stress have the same radius scaling, leaving a limiting mass of order (K/G)3/2 rather than allowing arbitrary mass to be supported by contraction. The Chandrasekhar limit is this maximum mass for a cold electron-degenerate star at specified composition, of order (ℏc/G)3/2/(μe​mp​)2.
The virial calculation by itself does not establish a universal numerical maximum mass for every stellar composition and equation of state; its precise consequence is loss of binding/support as the pressure-bearing particles become ultrarelativistic. An accreting carbon-oxygen white dwarf approaching its limiting mass typically undergoes runaway carbon burning and thermonuclear disruption, a Type Ia supernova. For other compositions or evolution, electron captures can instead lead to collapse into a neutron star. The subsequent evolution needs that physical distinction.

Every initial segment ending at (ξ,η) lies inside (max(ξ,η)+1)2. Its cardinal is less than κ, by the smaller-cardinal identity or finite counting. This well-order cannot have an element with κ predecessors, so its order type is at most the initial ordinal κ. Thus ∣κ×κ∣≤κ, contrary to its being a counterexample; the reverse injection is ξ↦(ξ,0). Hence

The path lifting theorem says that a path γ:[0,1]→X has a unique lift through a covering map once its initial point in the fiber is chosen. The homotopy lifting lemma says that a homotopy H:Z×[0,1]→X, with a continuous lift specified at time zero, has a unique continuous lifted homotopy. In particular a homotopy of paths with fixed endpoints preserves the endpoint of a chosen lift, since that endpoint varies continuously in a discrete fiber.
Choose x0​∈X and yi​∈pi−1​(x0​). For y∈Y1​, choose a path γ in Y1​ from y1​ to y, and let F(y) be the endpoint of the lift of p1​γ to Y2​ starting at y2​. Two choices of γ are homotopic relative endpoints because Y1​ is simply connected. Project that homotopy and apply homotopy lifting: the lifted endpoint remains fixed. Thus F is well-defined and p2​F=p1​.
To prove continuity without invoking covering-space classification, choose a path-connected open neighborhood U of p1​(y) evenly covered by both maps. Local path connectedness of X permits this choice. On the sheet of p1−1​(U) containing y, append paths within that sheet to the chosen path to y. Path-lift uniqueness gives
F=(p2​∣V2​​)−1∘p1​
(70)
there, for the sheet V2​ containing F(y). Hence F is a local homeomorphism and is continuous. Construct G:Y2​→Y1​ in the same way with the basepoints reversed. Lifting the very same projected paths proves GF and FG fix every point. Therefore
Y1​≅Y2​ by a homeomorphism commuting with the coverings.​
(71)

The Banach-Steinhaus theorem, or Uniform boundedness principle, states that for a family T of bounded linear operators from a Banach space E to a normed space F, pointwise boundedness supT∈T​∥Tx∥<∞ for every x∈E implies supT​∥T∥<∞.
For its proof let En​={x:supT​∥Tx∥≤n}. These are closed and their union is E. The Baire category theorem gives an En​ with nonempty interior, containing a ball B(x0​,r). For ∥h∥<r, both x0​ and x0​+h belong to En​, so ∥Th∥≤2n for every T. Scaling h and taking a limit at the ball boundary gives ∥T∥≤2n/r, proving the theorem. The target need not be complete.
For the asserted bounded-set criterion, use the Banach space X∗, which is complete even if X is not. Each x∈S defines the bounded linear evaluation functional Jx​(f)=f(x) on X∗. The given hypothesis says this family is pointwise bounded. The Hahn-Banach theorem consequence in the question gives ∥Jx​∥=∥x∥, and uniform boundedness yields
x∈Ssup​∥x∥<∞.​
(72)
This proves that weak boundedness implies norm boundedness; the two forms of boundedness coincide for a subset of a normed space.
Finally suppose the two continuous duals for ∥⋅∥1​ and ∥⋅∥2​ were equal as sets. The unit ball for norm two is bounded under every common continuous functional, using its norm-two continuity. Applying the preceding criterion in norm one bounds that ball in norm one; scaling gives ∥v∥1​≤C∥v∥2​. Reversing the roles gives ∥v∥2​≤C′∥v∥1​. The norms would be equivalent. Contrapositively, inequivalent norms have different continuous duals, supplying a linear functional continuous for one and discontinuous for the other.

Expanding the determinant, the coefficient multiplying ℘′(z) is ℘(−z−w)−A=O(z), so the apparent cubic pole reduces to order at most two. The only other possible pole is at z=−w, and f(−z−w)=−f(z) gives the same bound there. Thus, if f is nonconstant, its total pole order and valency are at most four. A constant case is handled by finding a zero below.
Column coincidences give zeros at z=w, at z=−2w, and at the four solutions of 2z=−w on C/Λ. The latter are distinct because Λ/2Λ has four elements. If 3w∈/Λ, the first two points are distinct from each other and from these four solutions.

Both the determinant and its first derivative vanish, since each term in the derivative still has two identical columns. Hence there are four distinct zeros, at least one multiple, giving at least five zeros counted with multiplicity.

A ring of sets is closed under finite unions and differences. A premeasure on it is a nonnegative set function with value zero on the empty set that is countably additive whenever a disjoint union remains in the ring. Caratheodory extension theorem extends a premeasure to a measure on the generated sigma-algebra; this extension is unique there when the premeasure is sigma-finite. It is obtained from the outer measure
μ∗(E)=inf{∑j​μ(Aj​):E⊆⋃j​Aj​, Aj​∈A},
(81)
whose measurable sets satisfy μ∗(E)=μ∗(E∩B)+μ∗(E∖B) for every E. The resulting complete measurable sigma-algebra contains the sigma-algebra generated by the ring.
For the required continuity, let Bn​↓∅ in the bounded-interval ring and fix ϵ>0. From each component (a,b] of Bn​, remove a sufficiently short initial piece and retain the compact interval [a+δ,b]. The union is a compact set Kn​⊂Bn​, and Bn​∖Kn​ is covered by a ring set Cn​ of total length less than ϵ2−n; one can take unions of (a,a+δ]. We do not incorrectly assume the compact sets themselves belong to the half-open interval ring.
Since ⋂n​Kn​=∅ and K1​ is compact, the finite intersection property supplies N with ⋂n=1N​Kn​=∅. For x∈BN​, membership in all earlier Bn​ means some failure of membership in Kn​ puts x in Cn​. Thus
BN​⊆⋃n=1N​Cn​,μ(BN​)≤∑n=1N​μ(Cn​)<ϵ.

A standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous sample paths, independent stationary increments, and Wt​−Ws​∼N(0,t−s) for t>s. The Brownian reflection principle reflects the increments after the first hitting time of a positive level and preserves Brownian law, by symmetry and the strong Markov property.
Reflect after the first hit of x. On the event that this hit occurs by time one, W1​ changes to 2x−W1​. This is a measure-preserving involution taking the event W1​≤x−y to W1​≥x+y, proving the specified identity for x>0,y≥0; the x=0 case follows by symmetry. With y=0, the maximum event splits, up to zero-probability equality, into reflected equal halves. Thus
P(M≥x)=2P(W1​≥x)=P(∣W1​∣≥x),x≥0.
(91)
Hence M and ∣W1​∣ have the same distribution, and M>0 almost surely.
For the ratio we need the joint law, not just these marginals. For w<m, the reflected identity gives P(M≥m,W1​≤w)=P(W1​≥2m−w). Differentiating yields
fM,W1​​(m,w)=2(2m−w)φ(2m−w),m>0,w<m,
(92)
where φ is the standard normal density. Put w=rm; the change of variables has Jacobian m. Therefore, for r<1,
fR​(r)=∫0∞​2(2−r)m2φ((2−r)m)dm=(2−r)22​∫0∞​v2φ(v)dv=(2−r)21​​.
(93)
The density is zero for r>1 and has no atom at one. Its integral on (−∞,1) is one; negative ratios have no lower bound.
This gives the complete Brownian terminal-to-maximum ratio law.

The eigenvalue one is impossible because A is invertible. Both quadratic forms are positive, so ∣λ∣<1. The splitting iteration Mx(k+1)=Nx(k)+b propagates its error by T; spectral radius less than one therefore gives convergence from every initial vector.

Words: 105
b OurBigBook.com
Write A=D+L+U, with D diagonal and L,U the strict triangular parts. The Jacobi method updates all coordinates using the preceding iterate:
x(k+1)=D−1(b−(L+U)x(k)).​
(138)
For a symmetric positive definite matrix, D has positive diagonal entries. In its splitting take M=D, N=D−A. The theorem requires M∗+N=2D−A to be positive definite, which need not hold for every positive definite matrix.
For this tridiagonal matrix, let S=diag((−1)1,…,(−1)n). Neighboring indices have opposite signs, so SAS=2D−A: the diagonal stays fixed and every nonzero off-diagonal entry changes sign. Thus
xT(2D−A)x=(Sx)TA(Sx)>0(x=0).
(139)
The Householder-John theorem now applies and proves Jacobi convergence for every initial vector. This is precisely why the tridiagonal structure matters.
